Cardiology and hematology · published research

Arterial restenosis

In one randomized cohort, intravascular laser improved selected angiographic lumen measures after coronary intervention. Restenosis and major cardiac events did not differ significantly, and later publications reused the same participants.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

During coronary intervention, intravascular laser may improve selected measures of lumen size. The effect on restenosis and major cardiac events remains uncertain, while laboratory and animal studies report biological responses across several protocols.

Summary of the Evidence

One randomized cohort found favorable changes in some angiographic measures after laser was delivered inside the coronary artery. The reduction in restenosis and major cardiac events was not statistically conclusive. Findings from animal and cell studies vary with the model and protocol.

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized study, 52 people received 808-nm laser illumination inside the coronary artery during percutaneous coronary intervention and 49 received PCI alone. Some lumen measurements favored laser, while differences in restenosis and major adverse cardiac events were not statistically conclusive (Derkacz et al. 2010).

Three later publications from the same cohort examined inflammatory cytokines, nitric oxide and endothelin-1, and growth factors. They add biological measurements rather than independent patient outcomes (Derkacz et al. 2013; Derkacz et al. 2014; Derkacz et al. 2017). A 2021 review used a PRISMA-aligned search across four databases and discussed the intracoronary study in relation to restenosis, but reported no pooled treatment estimate or new patient cohort (Colombo et al. 2021). Smaller single-arm reports and a two-case series add clinical experience but do not establish longer-term benefit (Kaul et al. 1998; Derkacz et al. 2003; Derkacz et al. 2005).

Animal evidence

Rabbit balloon-injury and atherosclerotic models report less neointimal growth or favorable lumen measures after endoluminal laser at selected settings. Pig coronary-stent studies report larger lumen dimensions or less neointimal area at selected red-light doses, with findings varying across dose protocols (Kipshidze et al. 1998; De Scheerder et al. 1998; Kipshidze et al. 2001; De Scheerder et al. 2001).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In-vitro studies report that 594–600 nm light inhibits vascular smooth-muscle-cell migration. A later human endothelial-cell study found wavelength- and exposure-dependent changes in migration and miR-143, including delayed miR-143 upregulation after 633-nm exposure (Deckelbaum et al. 1993; Asadi et al. 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical study used an 808-nm near-infrared laser delivered inside the coronary artery during PCI as a single treatment. Animal experiments used different catheter designs, models, wavelengths, and doses, including 632-nm red light in atherosclerotic rabbits, short-pulsed 1064-nm light in a rabbit injury model, and intravascular red light at several doses in pig stent models. Cell experiments used 594–600 nm or 532 and 633 nm at different exposure durations. These protocols do not identify an optimal clinical wavelength, fluence, power, or catheter position, and do not test repeated outpatient or transcutaneous treatment (Kipshidze et al. 1998; De Scheerder et al. 1998; Kipshidze et al. 2001; De Scheerder et al. 2001; Deckelbaum et al. 1993; Asadi et al. 2026).

Interpretation

Selected angiographic measures favored intravascular laser in one randomized cohort, but the results for restenosis and cardiac events were inconclusive. The later cohort reports add biological measurements rather than independent patient outcomes. Animal and cell findings support biological activity across several protocols but do not show fewer repeat procedures.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

In one randomized cohort of 101 people, restenosis at six months was 15.0% after intravascular laser and 32.4% with PCI alone; the difference was not statistically significant (Derkacz et al. 2010).

At six months, minimal lumen diameter was 2.18 ± 0.70 mm versus 1.76 ± 0.74 mm (p < 0.05), and late lumen loss was 0.53 ± 0.68 mm versus 0.76 ± 0.76 mm (p < 0.01). The late-loss index also favored laser (0.28 ± 0.39 vs 0.46 ± 0.43, p < 0.005) (Derkacz et al. 2010).

Major adverse cardiac events were not significantly different at six months (7.7% vs 14.3%) or twelve months (7.7% vs 18.5%).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low, limited and mixed clinical evidence for a clinical benefit from intravascular laser during coronary intervention. One randomized cohort found favorable changes in some lumen measures, but results for restenosis and major cardiac events were inconclusive.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Only one randomized cohort assessed clinical outcomes; later reports from the same participants measured biomarkers rather than independent treatment effects. Several angiographic measures favored laser, but restenosis and major cardiac-event differences were inconclusive. The evidence therefore gives limited confidence in a clinical benefit and does not show fewer repeat procedures or improved longer-term outcomes (Derkacz et al. 2010; Derkacz et al. 2017).
